Duval County offices behind a Jacksonville tax bill

Jacksonville and Duval County share a single tax collector. That office sends the bills and takes payments. A separate property appraiser decides what each parcel is worth and who gets an exemption.

  • Tax collector: 231 E. Forsyth Street, Jacksonville, FL 32202. Call (904) 255-5700 and choose option 4 for property tax. The main office is open weekdays from half past eight to half past four.
  • Property appraiser exemptions desk: (904) 255-5900, for homestead status and address changes.
  • Value Adjustment Board clerk: 117 West Duval Street, Suite 305, for formal appeals.

Branch offices are spread across the city. A St. Johns Square branch at 11160 Beach Blvd., Suite 121 took the place of the Kernan and Hogan locations in 2026. Call ahead for branch hours before you go in person.

Payment months and discounts

Jacksonville tax is figured on the January 1 value, mailed in November and due in full by March 31. Every month you wait shrinks the discount.

A Jacksonville house that goes under contract in spring has usually been billed already. Ask which discount tier the seller used and confirm the payment cleared.

What happens to delinquent accounts?

An account unpaid on April 1 carries a mandatory minimum interest fee of 3%, plus advertising costs. Whatever remains goes into the annual tax certificate sale, which has to take place on or before June 1. The collector sets the rules bidders follow:

  • The lowest interest rate wins, and ties are settled by random draw.
  • A deposit of $100 or 10% of intended bids, whichever is larger, must arrive five business days before the sale.
  • Winners pay within 48 hours or lose the deposit.
  • A certificate redeemed early pays the buyer at least 5%, whatever the bid was.
  • A certificate expires if no tax deed application follows within seven years.

Two other points matter more to an owner. Homestead liens are excluded from the certificate sale, and the Clerk of Court, not the collector, conducts tax deed sales. A tax deed is also not a warranty deed, so a buyer at that sale may have to clear title through a court action.

How does the Duval installment plan work?

If your estimated bill is over $100, you can split it into four payments by applying by April 30 of the year you want to start. Apply through your online account, by email to taxdept@coj.net, or by mail to Installment Processing at the Forsyth Street office.

  • First payment: June 30, 6% discount.
  • Second payment: September 30, 4.5% discount.
  • Third payment: December 31, 3% discount.
  • Fourth payment: March 31, no discount.

A July 31 row lets you make a late first payment with no discount. Miss that too and the account leaves the plan without penalty and is billed in November. After the first payment you are committed for the rest of the year, and a skipped installment is rolled into the next one with no discount. Enrolled accounts re-enter each year automatically. To pay only part of a bill outside the plan, speak to the tax collector first.

How to dispute a valuation or exemption

A petition to the Value Adjustment Board has to be received within 25 days of the mailing of your TRIM notice. The due date is printed in the lower right corner of the notice, and a postmark does not count: the board must physically have the petition and fee by then. Online filing closes at 11:59 p.m. on the deadline date. The pattern is an August notice and a September deadline. A late petition must come by hand or mail with a written good-cause explanation and documents.

  • Fee: up to $50 per parcel, not refundable.
  • Waiver: a homeowner who appeals a homestead denial on time pays nothing.
  • Form: DR-486, available from the board, the appraiser or the state.
  • Panel: two City Council members, one school board member and two citizens.

The appraiser invites an informal review first but cannot accept a petition itself.

Before filing, collect what supports your number: recent sales of similar homes, photos of any damage, and repair quotes. Write down the exact change you are asking for, whether that is a lower value or a restored exemption. Keep copies of everything you send, and note the date it was received.

Why two similar Jacksonville houses can carry different bills

Tax rates are usually the same on both. Taxable value is what differs. A long-time homesteader's assessed value has been held down by the Save Our Homes cap, which the state chart sets at 2.7 percent for 2026, while a recent buyer pays on full market value.

Other surprises have simple causes. A partial homestead exemption can come from multiple owners, mixed use or several buildings. A bank-sold house is still valued at market, because foreclosures and distressed sales are not treated as qualified sales. A homestead can show a rising assessed value even when market value fell, until the gap built up by the cap is used up.

When you sell, expect the buyer's first bill to climb. The change of ownership removes the cap, and the exemption has to be applied for again by March 1. The standard homestead exemption is up to $50,000, filed on DR-501.

Settling tax when the house sells

Ask the tax collector for a written payoff and pass it to the title company. The closing agent subtracts what is owed and apportions the current year across both parties. If you are on the installment plan, ask the collector what happens to the remaining payments.

  • Ask whether the account carries back taxes or a certificate.
  • Check the bill for non-ad valorem lines such as stormwater and solid waste.
  • Search the clerk's Official Records for recorded liens.

Florida's deed stamp tax is 70 cents on each $100 of consideration, and any party named on the deed can be held liable. Recording is priced under s. 28.24: $5.00 on page one, $4.00 on each later page, and added per-page charges.

Keep your parcel number and a copy of the deed handy when you call any office, and get every balance quoted with a date. A seller facing back tax or damage may prefer a cash buyer who accepts the house as-is, with the title company clearing the tax from proceeds. Cash also skips lender appraisal and underwriting.

Where to find the Jacksonville millage rate

Millage charts are posted by the Property Appraiser. A mill equals $1 of tax per $1,000 of taxable value, and your parcel's total adds up each district's rate. Use your own bill or the appraiser's chart rather than a citywide guess.

Frequently asked questions

When does Jacksonville tax become delinquent?

April 1 of the year after the assessment. A minimum 3% interest fee and advertising costs follow, and unpaid accounts move toward a certificate sale held by June 1.

What discount do I get for paying a Jacksonville bill early?

November payments get 4%, December 3%, January 2% and February 1%. March payments get none.

Are homesteads sold in the Duval tax certificate sale?

No. Homestead liens are excluded from the sale. The tax itself must still be paid.

Who do I call about a Jacksonville bill that looks wrong?

Start with the property appraiser's exemptions line, (904) 255-5900. If that fails, petition the Value Adjustment Board before the notice's printed deadline. Payment plans are a question for the collector.

How is a Jacksonville house's tax divided at closing?

The closing statement shows each side's share, and unpaid back tax comes out of the seller's proceeds. Get the payoff figure in writing beforehand.

Which office sends the bill and which sets the value

The Miami-Dade Tax Collector prints and collects the bill. The Property Appraiser of Miami-Dade County produces the values behind it and never mails bills or sets and collects taxes. Miami levies its own mills, and they appear on the same statement as county, school and special district lines.

The city spreads across 36.00 square miles, and parcels in different neighborhoods can sit on different taxing lines. Work from the folio number, not the street address.

  • Appraiser, downtown: Stephen P. Clark Center, 111 NW 1st Street, Suite 710, 305-375-4712, weekdays 8 to 5.
  • Appraiser, south: South Dade Government Center, 10710 SW 211 Street, Cutler Bay, 305-232-3810.
  • Tax Collector: payments online at any hour, at 13 locations, or through its T-Connect mobile offices.

Services you can finish without a trip downtown

More can be done remotely than the old paper routine suggests. The appraiser takes widow(er) exemptions and disability exemptions for a veteran or surviving spouse online, with document upload. Agricultural classification applications on Form MD-482 can be filed the same way. A tangible personal property search covers business accounts by name, address or folio, and appointments at the downtown and Cutler Bay offices can be booked online.

The clerk offers a free alert that emails an owner within 24 hours when a deed or mortgage is recorded in that owner's name. A house left vacant after a move or a death is a common target for deed fraud, so enroll before you list.

The county's 2026 adopted millage chart shows Miami at 7.1080 mills for city operations plus 0.2536 for city debt, for a row total of 19.9544. The 2025 column for the same row reads 19.9878, so the combined figure slipped by 0.0334.

A second row covers the downtown development area. Houses inside that boundary pay an added 0.3800, bringing the total to 20.3344 (20.3778 in 2025). Confirm your parcel on the appraiser's site before you quote either row.

Miami's housing mix

Only 30.8 percent of Miami housing units are lived in by their owners, so investor-held houses are common. A landlord selling has no homestead relief to lose, and an owner-occupant buying from one can apply after closing. The typical owner-reported value is $518,100, and median gross rent is $1,758.

Amendment 3 and the estimator

The appraiser's home page offers a property tax estimator tied to the Amendment 3 changes, with separate results for 2027 and 2028. Those years match the statewide measure voters passed on November 3, 2026. The 2026 bill now in hand is unchanged, and the Tax Collector's pay-early campaign, built around the 4 percent November discount, applies to it.

Run the estimator for the year your closing or purchase falls in. A buyer who expects a larger exemption should still file for it, since benefits reach an owner only through an application. Dates to remember: April 1 is when unpaid bills turn delinquent, and the discount runs November through February.

What a Miami seller should collect before closing

Bring four things: the folio number, the August TRIM notice showing proposed taxes, proof of each exemption on file, and a Tax Collector payoff letter for any open year.

A house inside the downtown development area needs the title agent's attention because of the extra 0.3800 mills. Buyers should expect the first bill after purchase to start from just value, which can run well above the seller's bill.

Homestead and portability

Apply on Form DR-501 by March 1 for a house that was your permanent home on January 1. Renting it ends the benefit. A sale restarts the buyer at just value, and the seller can port savings to a new Florida homestead with Form DR-501T inside three years.

Suspected homestead abuse can be reported to the appraiser's compliance unit at 305-375-3402. An owner who cannot pay at once can ask the Tax Collector about deferral on Form DR-570 (March 31) or installments (May 1).

Selling with back taxes

After April 1 the account is delinquent, and a certificate is sold by June 1. The certificate buyer must wait two years before pressing the owner. A tax deed application costs $75, and a homestead parcel's opening bid includes half of the latest assessed value. If no one bids, the county has 90 days to take the land at the opening bid.

A seller with arrears can still close, because the title company pays the lien from proceeds. Request the payoff early, and call the Tax Collector long before any auction date.

A sensible order of steps

Selling a house goes more smoothly when the tax and title chores are done in a set order. These are general steps, not rules specific to one office.

  1. Pull your parcel record and confirm the owner name, mailing address and exemptions are right.
  2. Find out whether any tax year is open and ask for a written payoff figure.
  3. Search the recorded documents under every name on the deed for unreleased mortgages or liens.
  4. Gather your latest statement and the proposed-tax notice for the buyer and the title agent.
  5. Agree in the contract on how the current year's tax will be split.
  6. At closing, review the settlement statement line by line before you sign.

If a step turns up a problem, raise it with the title agent early. Most issues are routine to clear when found before a buyer is waiting.

What a cash sale skips

A cash sale takes the lender out of the picture. There is no appraisal for a mortgage, no loan underwriting and no financing contingency that can fall through late. The seller still has the same tax and title duties: open taxes are paid from proceeds, recorded liens are released, and the deed is signed, witnessed, notarized and recorded.

Compare any offer with the payoff figures in your own records. The net to you is the price minus the payoffs, the tax proration and closing costs, so ask for a written estimate of those numbers before you agree to a date.

Where Miami deeds are recorded

Deeds go to the Miami-Dade County Recorder's Office, 20 NW 1st Avenue, Suite 5.246, run by the county clerk. The clerk's checklist asks for the seller's original signature, two unrelated witnesses with printed names and addresses, a notary acknowledgement and a Prepared By line. Before the notary meeting, compare the folio and legal description with the prior deed, and have the witnesses' printed names and addresses ready. Deed stamps run 60 cents per $100 here.

Frequently asked questions

Is Miami's city millage rate 7.1080?

Yes, for city operations on the county's 2026 chart, plus 0.2536 for city debt. All authorities total 19.9544 mills, or 20.3344 on the downtown development line.

Can a Miami landlord claim homestead?

No. The owner must live in the home as a permanent residence by January 1, and renting the unit ends the exemption.

What early payment discount does a Miami bill carry?

It steps down monthly from 4 percent for November to 1 percent for February. March is due at the full amount.

Does the Miami property appraiser collect tax?

No. The appraiser neither sends bills nor sets or collects taxes. Payments go to the Miami-Dade Tax Collector.

How do I check my Miami taxable value?

Search by address, owner name or folio on the appraiser's site, or call 305-375-4712 to book an assessment review.

Who sends which bill

Property tax in Miami Beach involves three desks. The county Property Appraiser sets the value and handles exemptions. The county Tax Collector mails the yearly statement and takes payment. Miami Beach Finance, at 1700 Convention Center Drive, bills the city's own charges: utilities, special assessments and Resort Tax.

Finance keeps weekday hours of 9AM to 5PM, with a customer service window from 8:30AM to 6PM. The main number is 305.673.7000, and Resort Tax questions go to 305.673.7420.

  • Valuation, exemption filings and portability: county Property Appraiser.
  • Annual statement, tax certificate sales and 13 payment locations: county Tax Collector.
  • Water, sewer and storm bills, plus assessments recorded against the lot: Miami Beach Finance.
  • Rentals taxed on room revenue: the Resort Tax desk at Finance.

The city also posts its budget documents, including the capital plan for nearby streets and seawalls, on its Office of Management and Budget page. An owner worried about a neighborhood project can read the schedule there.

Miami Beach millage for 2026

The county's 2026 adopted millage chart gives Miami Beach a city operating rate of 5.8060 mills and a voted debt rate of 0.2693 mills. The main Miami Beach line totals 18.6681. A second line carries the same city numbers, adds 0.7364 under a miscellaneous heading and totals 19.4045. The district code on your bill tells you which line you are on.

The rest of each total is the countywide, school, library, children's trust and regional stack, the same for every municipality. The city columns are where the differences show.

Short-term rentals and your homestead

Renting a Miami Beach home short term can cost the owner the homestead exemption. The city's business tax receipt paperwork includes a written notice, signed by the owner, saying the owner understands that short-term use could end the exemption.

The application also asks for a long document list. If you are selling a unit that has been run as a rental, or buying one, expect these items:

  • An approved Certificate of Use and a recorded warranty deed or bill of sale.
  • For condos, an association letter dated within the last 60 days confirming short-term rental is allowed for that unit.
  • Names and contacts for every hosting or advertising platform used for the listing.
  • A Resort Tax registration with photo ID and signatures of all operators.
  • A notarized affidavit, returned by mail or in person within two weeks of issuance.

Resort Tax is 4 percent on room rent and 2 percent on food and drink sales. A buyer underwriting a rental should price that in next to the property tax.

The city assigns occupational code 95017300 to residential short-term rental and 95017301 to the non-residential version, and the code decides which documents apply. A condo unit cannot get its own receipt until the association holds an active one. Before you advertise the income as transferable, check that the seller's receipt, Resort Tax account and association letter are all current. Ask Finance how sales through third-party platforms are reported.

Deadlines and discounts

Florida's statewide calendar sets the rhythm. Exemption papers reach the appraiser by March 1. The August mailing shows proposed taxes and opens a 25-day window to petition on value. November statements carry a 4 percent early discount that steps down monthly to 1 percent in February.

The Miami-Dade Tax Collector promotes the November date as "Save the Max" and takes payment online, at 13 locations and through T-Connect mobile offices. Anything open on April 1 goes delinquent, and certificates are sold by June 1.

How Save Our Homes treats a Miami Beach house

Homestead takes up to $50,000 off taxable value and is filed on Form DR-501. After the first year, assessed value may rise by the smaller of 3 percent or the CPI change. The state's cap chart shows 2.9 percent for 2025 and 2.7 percent for 2026.

The cap ends at sale, because the next owner starts at full just value on the following January 1. A seller moving to another Florida home can apply portability on that replacement home with Form DR-501T inside a three-year window.

What gets settled at a Miami Beach closing?

The title agent reconciles the year's county bill, utility balances and any city assessment on the lot. Ask Finance for a payoff on the city items, since the county statement does not show them.

Miami-Dade deeds carry their own stamp tax rate: 60 cents per $100, plus a 45 cents per $100 surtax that skips a deed conveying only a single-family dwelling. The Miami-Dade Clerk records the deed, and Florida requires two subscribing witnesses on a land conveyance.

On closing day the usual order is simple. The title agent confirms the payoff figures, the seller signs the deed before a notary and the required witnesses, funds are disbursed, and the deed goes to the clerk for recording. Ask for a copy of the settlement statement and keep it with your tax records for the year of sale.

Checking a listing's tax district

A buyer comparing two Miami Beach listings should look at the taxing district code and the folio's last bill, not only the city name. The extra 0.7364 on the second chart line adds roughly four percent to that line's total, and nobody can see it from the street address.

  • Pull the folio from the Property Appraiser and note its district.
  • Match it against the chart's line for Miami Beach.
  • Ask Finance whether a special assessment is recorded against the lot.
  • Use the Tax Collector's calculators to test a purchase price before making an offer.

Steps before you list

A few ordinary steps save time once a buyer appears. Gather your latest county statement and any city utility or assessment notices. Ask the title company for an early payoff and proration estimate. Confirm the owner name and mailing address on the appraiser's record. If a loan was paid off, check that the release was recorded. Then share the list with your agent or closing attorney so nothing surfaces late in the deal.

A seller who sells for cash to a buyer taking the home as is can skip repair negotiations and lender timelines, but taxes, assessments and utility balances still get paid from proceeds at closing.

Frequently asked questions

Does the City of Miami Beach send the property tax bill?

No. The Miami-Dade Tax Collector bills property tax. Miami Beach Finance bills utilities and special assessments and collects Resort Tax.

What are the Miami Beach city millage numbers for 2026?

The chart shows 5.8060 mills operating and 0.2693 voted debt, with totals of 18.6681 and 19.4045 on its two Miami Beach lines.

Can renting my condo short term affect my homestead?

Yes. The city requires owners to acknowledge in writing that short-term rental use could cause loss of the homestead exemption.

What is the Resort Tax rate in Miami Beach?

It is 4 percent on room rent and 2 percent on restaurant, bar and nightclub sales.

Who do I ask about a special assessment on my lot?

Call Miami Beach Finance at 305.673.7000. The department invoices and collects all special assessments.

Homestead exemption savings

Owners who qualify can take as much as $50,000 off assessed value, split into two slices. Only the first $25,000 applies to school taxes, while the second slice covers value above $50,000. Residence on January 1 is required, and Form DR-501 goes to the Property Appraiser by March 1.

  • Renting the house out, or ceasing to be a Florida resident, ends the exemption.
  • Save Our Homes limits each year's rise in assessed value to 3 percent or inflation, whichever is less. The state's chart shows 2.7 percent for 2026.
  • After title changes hands, the next January 1 resets value to just value, with a few spouse and inheritance exceptions.
  • Portability carries some of the capped savings to a new Florida homestead. File DR-501T, and set up the new home within three years of the January 1 after you left the old one.

Buyers can run the Property Appraiser's online tax estimator before making an offer.

What can an owner do about a value or exemption notice?

Each August the Property Appraiser mails TRIM notices. You have 25 days from that mailing to petition the Value Adjustment Board, or 30 days from a denial letter if an exemption was refused.

Filing the exemption on time spares you an appeal. Should a ruling by the appraiser or the board produce a refund, the collector's FAQ lists an email address for it. Money owed back because of a sale is handled separately, between buyer and seller at closing.

City of Homestead millage and bonds

The city's approved FY 2026 to 2027 budget leaves the operating millage rate where it was the year before. Total millage on any parcel is the sum of every taxing district, so read the rate on your own notice.

On November 4, 2025, the city put two general obligation bonds to voters, one for parks and one for roads. The city's FAQ estimated 0.3661 mills for parks and 0.3983 mills for roadways if all of it were issued, with borrowing in several series. Ask the city whether either bond now shows on your parcel.

Paying the bill and finding older records

The collector takes payment online by check, credit card or debit card. In person it accepts check, cashier's check, money order, certified funds, cash, cards or Apple Pay. By mail, write the folio number and a phone number on a check made out to the Miami-Dade County Office of the Tax Collector in U.S. funds, and leave out sensitive details.

  • Wire payments: email the wire address on the collector's FAQ page for instructions. A wire takes one to two business days to post.
  • Older bills: the collector can supply tax records older than those online, and the FAQ lists an email address for the request.
  • Escrow: if you are unsure whether your lender is paying, ask the lender directly.
  • Roll changes: the certified tax roll reaches the collector once a year, around November 1, so recent ownership or address changes may not show online before then.

Florida has no personal property tax on vehicles, which spares a seller who is also moving a car or boat from one more bill. Before you wire or mail a large payment, confirm the folio number and the tax year on the notice so the money lands on the right account, and keep the receipt for the closing file.

Before closing on a Homestead house

Miami-Dade uses its own deed stamp rate: 60 cents per $100 plus a 45-cent surtax, with the surtax skipped on a document transferring only a single-family dwelling. Most other counties charge 70 cents per $100. Every party to a document can be held liable.

  • Order a written payoff and ask if any delinquency or certificate notice is on file.
  • Find out from the title company how your share of the year will be calculated.
  • Review the clerk's records for liens and check for a Water, Road and Sewer assessment.
  • Report any quarterly installment payments already made, since missing the July 31 first-payment cutoff removes the account from the plan.

Bring the folio number and a copy of your deed when you contact any office, and get each balance quoted in writing with a date, since amounts shift during the year. Ask the title company to confirm that every earlier year is paid, not just the current bill. If you make installment payments, hand the closing agent the receipts. When back taxes or a title problem would stall a buyer who needs a bank loan, a cash purchase lets the title company clear the debt from your proceeds without waiting on lender approval.

Frequently asked questions

Who bills a house in the City of Homestead?

The Miami-Dade County Office of the Tax Collector. The city sets a rate but does not send a bill.

When is Homestead real estate tax late?

After March 31. April 1 brings at least 3% interest plus advertising costs and fees.

Does a tax certificate mean the city takes my house?

Not yet. The certificate is a lien an investor buys, and a deed application cannot come until two years after that April 1.

Do I qualify for the exemption if I move in during the spring?

Not for that year. You must live there on January 1 and file by March 1, and a sale resets the buyer's assessed value the next January 1.

Does the City of Homestead add its own transfer tax?

Ask the city whether any local charge applies. The state deed stamp tax applies at the Miami-Dade rate.

A mill is a dollar of tax for every thousand dollars of taxable value. Your notice prints the city's rate beside the county, school and special district rates.

The Property Appraiser publishes final millage sheets each year comparing the City of Tampa, Temple Terrace, Plant City and unincorporated Hillsborough County. Each column covers one taxing area, so use the column that matches your parcel. Later years get a new resolution each time, so check the current number with the tax office at the time you sell.

Due dates and discounts

Watch for your TRIM notice by the end of August. It shows estimated just value as of January 1. To dispute the value, you have 25 days from the proposed-tax notice to file a petition with the clerk. A denied exemption carries its own 30 day limit, counted from the date the denial letter went out.

  • Exemption and classification applications close March 1.

If your notice looks wrong, phone the appraiser at 813-272-6100 before the deadline passes. Renting out a homesteaded house can end the exemption, so tell the office if your use has changed.

How a sale changes the tax on a Tampa house

Buyers often pay more than sellers did. Homestead growth is capped at 3% a year, but the cap lasts only through the year of purchase. Then the home is reassessed at market value. You may owe a prorated share of your own tax at closing, while the next year's assessment reflects the new market value.

Whichever is lower, 3% or the CPI change, sets the cap. Selling counts as a change of ownership, so the property resets on the next January 1 and your bill tells a buyer little.

  • Homestead ends once the house is no longer your permanent residence.
  • With portability, part of the saved value follows you to another Florida home, provided the new homestead is set up within three years of January 1 of the year you gave up the old one.

Older homes and neighborhoods

Older Tampa neighborhoods went up in distinct waves, and a home's age and location steer the questions buyers ask. Ybor City, shaped by the cigar trade, spans about two square miles between Nebraska Avenue, 22nd Street, Columbus Drive and East Broadway. A building boom from 1923 to 1926 created many subdivisions, among them Davis Island where the Hillsborough River meets the bay. Downtown condos and townhomes draw a different crowd than bungalow streets do.

Older houses invite questions about repairs and permits. Before you start any work, ask the City of Tampa about permits and historic district rules, and pull the permit record so an inspector's questions get answered with paper.

On a deed, Florida charges documentary stamp tax of 70 cents for each $100 of consideration. It is collected by the clerk at recording, and every signer on the document is answerable.

  • Have the closing agent prorate this year's tax.
  • File away a copy of the signed closing statement.

If taxes stay unpaid, they can be sold as a certificate, and its holder may apply for a tax deed two years on. Pay off any late year before saying yes to an offer.

Steps from listing to closing

Begin by checking the parcel record on the appraiser's site for the right owner name, legal description and exemptions. Next, pull your latest tax bill and any mortgage statement. Once you have an offer, the title company searches for liens and judgments and asks the Tax Collector for a payoff on any open year.

At closing you sign the deed, the agent prorates this year's tax, and the clerk records the deed with the stamp tax paid. Afterward, tell the appraiser the house has sold so your homestead comes off the roll, and file Form DR-501T by March 1 if you are buying another Florida home. A cash offer skips the lender's appraisal, so these same steps can finish in less time, yet nothing on this list goes away.

Selling a Tampa house when taxes are behind

Yes. Back taxes come out of the sale, normally from your proceeds. Request a payoff from the Tax Collector and list it with any mortgage payoff as you compare offers. A buyer taking the house as is can close without repairs, which helps when money is tight.

Paying off the balance before listing is easy to do. The collector takes payment online at HillsTaxFL.gov with a free e-Check, by mail, at 24/7 drop boxes and at service centers. Get the exact payoff in writing first.

Compare a direct sale against listing, considering commissions, repairs, months of carrying cost and how much delinquent tax accrues in the meantime. Whichever route you pick, take your deed, latest tax bill and mortgage statement to the title company so it can order the search at once. A cash buyer skips lender underwriting, but the title work and payoffs still set the closing date.

What is the City of Tampa's property tax rate?

6.2076 mills for fiscal year 2026, under Resolution 2025-813. That is only the city's share, and other authorities show up as separate lines.

When are Tampa property taxes due?

Pay the 2026 roll by March 31, 2027. Paying by November 30, 2026 saves 4%, by December 31 saves 3%, by January 31 saves 2% and by February 28 saves 1%.

Who do I call about my Tampa property value or exemptions?

Value and exemption questions go to the appraiser at 813-272-6100. For payments, call the Tax Collector at 813-635-5200.

Does the homestead cap carry over to the buyer in Tampa?

No. The cap holds through the year of purchase only, and then the home is reassessed at market value.

Who pays documentary stamp tax on a Tampa deed?

The state holds every party on the deed liable, whatever the contract says. The rate is 70 cents per $100, collected at recording.

The city millage rate

Orlando's own rate is 0.00665, or 6.65 mills, and the city reports it has not moved in over ten years. One mill equals a tenth of a cent per dollar of taxable value. Treat it as a single line item: the county, the school system and the water district each add their own, and special assessments sit below those.

The Property Appraiser posts the final millage for every taxing body by year. To see what a particular address pays, pull its actual bill from the Tax Collector. Neighborhoods and special taxing districts produce different totals.

Orlando housing at a glance

The city counts about 333,888 residents, 8.4 percent more than in 2020, spread over 131,179 households. Fewer than half of those households own, and the median value of an owned home is $394,100. A rejected exemption has its own window of 30 days after the denial letter goes out, and that petition is directed to the value adjustment board. Public hearings by the taxing bodies fill September and October, and the final statements follow in November.

The lid and the savings it built are tied to you rather than to the property. What to bring when you call the offices

A short call goes faster with details in hand. Have the parcel ID or the street address, the name exactly as it appears on the deed, and the most recent statement. If you are weighing a standard listing against a quick cash sale, ask the same questions either way. The tax picture on the parcel does not change with the sale route, and a clean payoff figure makes both options simpler.

A simple checklist before you list

Do these in order. Look up the parcel at the Property Appraiser and check that the owner names and exemptions are right. Then open the Tax Collector's account page and write down which years show paid. If a balance is open, ask for the payoff letter. Last, collect your most recent statement and the August notice so the title agent has them.

Also decide how the current year will be split with the buyer and say so to your closing agent. November bills and year-round closings do not line up, so the contract should spell out who covers the months each side owned the home.

No. The Orange County Tax Collector sends one bill that includes the city's levy. Orlando sets its own millage rate and keeps about 35 cents of each dollar.

On April 1. The full amount is due by March 31, and payment must reach the Tax Collector by then. A 3 percent minimum charge and advertising cost follow.

Does my homestead cap carry over when I sell in Orlando?

No. A sale resets assessed value to just value the next January 1. You may carry part of the benefit to a new Florida homestead through portability, filed by March 1.

Who bills property tax in Cape Coral

Cape Coral is inside Lee County, so the Lee County Tax Collector mails and collects your bill, and the Lee County Property Appraiser sets the value and rules on exemptions. The city's part is limited to its own millage rate and its special assessments.

Knowing the split saves phone time. Value, mailing address and exemption questions go to the appraiser's office at 239-533-6100. Payments, receipts and refunds go to the tax collector. A question about one specific levy goes to the authority named on that line of the bill.

The city has about 236,264 residents, up 21.8% since the 2020 base, and owners occupy 77.2% of homes. Typical home value is $373,500. With that much growth, many sellers hold older, capped assessments, and the people buying from them start from a reset value.

What the city adds on top of the county

Cape Coral levies its own operating millage. Council kept it at 5.1471 mills in the Fiscal Year 2027 budget approved at the September 24 hearing. A mill is one dollar of tax on every thousand dollars of taxable value, and the city rate is only one line among several authorities on your bill.

When you sell in Cape Coral

Compare the settlement statement against your bill line by line. If something looks off, raise it before closing day, because corrections are easier to make while the file is still open. Keep copies of every payment confirmation, and write down who you spoke with at each office and when. If you inherit or buy a second Cape Coral parcel, run the same checks on it separately, since each parcel has its own bill, its own exemptions and its own payoff. If you plan to sell to a cash buyer, the same payoff figure applies, though there is no lender waiting on an appraisal or underwriting, so a clear tax record tends to speed things up.

Council kept the operating millage at 5.1471 in the Fiscal Year 2027 budget approved on September 24. Your total bill adds county, school and other authorities, so check your parcel on the tax collector's site.

When are Lee County taxes delinquent?

Delinquency begins April 1, right after the March 31 due date. Once a bill is delinquent, the tax collector won't take a personal check or eCheck.

Does the installment plan transfer when I sell?

The buyer takes it over. A new owner continues the plan for that tax year once installments have started, so settle in the contract who owes the remainder.

Which offices to deal with

A Fort Myers owner works with two county offices. One decides what your property is worth: the Lee County Property Appraiser. The other mails the bill and receives your check: the Lee County Tax Collector.

Questions on value, exemptions or a changed mailing address go to leepa.org or 239-533-6100. For anything about paying, dial 239-533-6000. Your bill also names each authority that levies a tax, and those authorities answer for their own ad valorem rates and non-ad valorem assessments.

Due dates and discounts

You can start paying November 1. The last day for the full amount is March 31 of the next year.

The best discount goes to November payers at 4 percent, then it steps down to 3 in December, 2 in January and 1 in February. Once April 1 arrives, any open balance is governed by the delinquent-tax statutes.

Ways to pay

There are six ways to pay in Lee County.

  • Online through its pay site, with a printable receipt.
  • Kiosks at any of six service centers, by card or e-check; e-check payments are free.
  • Secure SmartLockers at the downtown Fort Myers, South Fort Myers, Cape Coral and Lehigh Acres centers, open around the clock. The Bonita Springs center takes drop-offs inside during business hours. Allow five business days.
  • By phone at 239-533-6000.
  • By mail, following the instructions on the bill.
  • In person at a service center.

The office posts payments within two business days after receiving them, and your account history online reads PAID or UNPAID.

Installments, partial payments and deferral

Three arrangements let you pay over time or put off a bill, and the rules differ for each.

Lee County payment plans
PlanMain terms
Installment planApply November 1 to April 30; taxes over $100 per notice; four payments due June 30, September 30, December 31 and March 31, with discounts of 6, 4.5 and 3 percent on the first three

For the 2027 tax year you can apply between November 1, 2026 and April 30, 2027. Should the home sell partway through, the buyer must keep the plan going for the rest of that year.

Missing an installment

Miss the first installment deadline of July 31 and you are out of the plan. A normal notice goes out by November 1, and you will have to apply again next year.

  • If you skip the second or third payment, that amount is added to the next one.
  • A late installment of any kind costs you its discount.
  • Payment one equals a quarter of last year's gross tax; later payments can include half of any change to this year's taxes.
  • You stay enrolled from year to year so long as the first installment gets paid each time.

Any amount still owing on April 1 moves into the delinquent-tax process.

Amendment 3

Your 2026 bill, due by March 31, 2027, is unaffected by Amendment 3. The amendment starts January 1, 2027, so whatever it changes will first appear on next year's bills. For its effect on your exemptions or assessment, ask the Lee County Property Appraiser.

The August notice

In August you receive the TRIM notice (Form DR-474), a preview of proposed taxes. Public hearings on tentative budgets and millage follow in September and October, and final budgets and rates are heard in October and November.

The actual bill is mailed in November. Anyone contesting a value must file with the clerk inside 25 days of the notice. A surprise on the notice leaves you time to review your exemptions with the appraiser before the bill shows up.

Assessment limits

Under Save Our Homes a homestead can gain no more than 3 percent or CPI in a year, whichever is less; the state chart shows 2.9 percent for 2025. Other property may rise 10 percent annually.

The appraiser's home page carries short videos about homestead and portability, the non-homestead limitation and estimating your taxes. Watch them before a sale or purchase, since the property resets to just value when it changes hands and the cap begins again.

Homestead exemption

Up to $50,000 of value comes off the taxable amount, in two pieces. The opening $25,000 lowers every levy, schools included. A second piece of up to $25,000 begins above $50,000 of assessed value and relieves only non-school levies.

  • The form is DR-501, and it goes to the appraiser by March 1.
  • The home must be your permanent residence on January 1.
  • Renting the unit, moving out for good or leaving Florida ends the exemption.
  • Older, disabled and military owners may have extra relief; ask the appraiser.

Taxes when the house sells

The bill for the whole year is addressed to the owner of record. Dividing it between buyer and seller is the closing agent's job.

The new deed is recorded with the Clerk of Court and then forwarded to the appraiser, and that lag explains why a seller can still receive a bill. An old mortgage company may also still be printed on the notice, so check that no escrow money is left. Your buyer files a separate homestead application by March 1.

To get ready, collect your deed, ID and latest tax bill, and pass the collector's payoff figure to the title agent. Read the draft settlement statement several days before the closing date. Cash buyers skip loan underwriting, so their closings can run on a shorter schedule.

If a bill goes unpaid

April 1 makes a balance delinquent. The collector then auctions a certificate against the parcel by June 1, and the bidder willing to take the lowest interest rate wins, with bids falling in quarter-percent steps.

  • For two years after that April 1, the certificate holder has no claim on the owner.
  • Then a tax deed can be requested, for a $75 application fee.
  • The clerk conducts the auction, where the high bidder leaves a deposit of 5 percent or $200, whichever is larger.

A sale that closes before any of this starts keeps the payoff simple. If a certificate already exists, ask the collector for a redemption amount good through your closing date, and pass it to the title agent so it can be paid from your proceeds.

Rental property

Furniture, appliances and other tangible personal property used when a home is rented can produce a separate tangible tax bill.

If you recently bought a home that is no longer rented, call the property appraiser's tangible office at 239-533-6140. Renting out a homestead can also end the exemption under state rules.

Frequently asked questions

How do I pay Lee County tax on a Fort Myers home?

Pay the Lee County Tax Collector online, by phone at 239-533-6000, by mail, or at a service center. Six service centers have kiosks.

Which office handles exemption questions?

Call 239-533-6100, the appraiser's number. Exemptions, values and mailing addresses are handled there.

When does the installment plan application close?

It closes April 30 of the tax year, and applications for 2027 taxes opened November 1, 2026. The first payment is due by June 30.

Why did I get a bill after selling?

The roll lists the owner of record when bills go out, and a recent sale may not have reached the appraiser yet. Pass the bill to the buyer or closing agent.

Can I pay delinquent Fort Myers taxes by check?

Not by personal check or eCheck. Ask the collector which payment forms it accepts for delinquent real estate taxes.

Who sends a Tallahassee homeowner the tax bill

The Leon County Tax Collector mails it, using a roll the Leon County Property Appraiser builds. A Tallahassee notice stacks the city's levy on top of county and other lines, and each body picks its own millage. The city line is not separate paperwork for you.

The appraiser multiplies values by the millage rates, then certifies the finished roll for printing. Corrections to a name, mailing address or location go to the appraiser. Fix any error before listing, since a buyer's lender will pull the same record. If your lender pays from escrow, have the lender request the original notice from the collector, and you will get a duplicate.

City millage and the fire assessment

The city's budget book lists 4.4072 mills for fiscal year 2026, within the 10.0 mill ceiling Florida allows a city. A mill means one dollar for every thousand of taxable value. County, school board and other lines come on top.

Tallahassee has an odd tax base. Government entities own over half the real property within city limits, and that land pays nothing. To make up for fire protection on those parcels, the city bills a non-ad valorem fire assessment, mostly through the monthly utility statement.

  • Homes pay the fire assessment per dwelling unit.
  • Commercial and other non-residential parcels pay by square footage tier.
  • Electricity sales in the city carry a 10% public service tax, leaving out the fuel adjustment charge.

The appraiser sends the city a preliminary value estimate in June and a final one in July, certified July 1. Two public budget hearings follow in September.

Due dates and penalties

Bills start going out on November 1 and the tax must be paid before April 1. On April 1 the collector adds a delinquency fee, an advertising fee and interest at 1.5 percent a month, plus statutory collection costs. A list of delinquent owners must be advertised locally within 45 days.

Homestead exemption

For tax year 2026 the exemption is up to $51,411 off assessed value. The first $25,000 reaches every tax, school included. A second slice of up to $26,411 sits on value over $50,000 and skips school taxes. Amendment 5, passed in 2024, indexes that second slice to the CPI.

Ownership and permanent residence on January 1 are required, March 1 is the filing deadline, and nothing happens automatically. The appraiser's office estimates savings around $800 a year.

  • After the first qualifying year, a Save Our Homes cap holds yearly assessed growth to 3% or the CPI change, whichever is smaller.
  • A sale restores the home to just value on the next January 1.
  • If you move, you can carry part of the saved difference to the next Florida homestead within three years, filing DR-501T.

City permits and utility accounts

Permits and utility accounts are the city-level items. A building permit is needed for construction, additions, alterations or repairs when labor and materials run over $1,000, residential or commercial. If you did work yourself or hired a handyman, look up the permit history before listing, then ask the city's permit staff how to close anything left open.

The city also bills electric, gas, water, sewer, stormwater and trash, so schedule final readings around closing. Single-family service, which covers properties of up to six units, includes weekly curbside pickup with a 96-gallon garbage cart and a 64-gallon recycling cart, and curbside trash and bulk waste every second week.

  • Stormwater charges follow an equivalent residential unit.
  • Rates for electric, gas, water, sewer and stormwater rise each October 1 with the CPI under the city code.
  • Fire assessments appear on utility bills for most city customers.

Your tax bill is one piece, and your city utility statement carries fire, trash and stormwater charges that a buyer will want settled cleanly at transfer. Ask the city utility office about final billing when you set a closing date.

How taxes are settled when you sell

Your closing agent prorates this year's bill and clears older unpaid years from your proceeds. Phone the collector for a payoff on any delinquent year, because interest runs every month after April 1. Unpaid accounts go to a certificate sale by June 1, and a certificate holder may seek a tax deed after two years.

The deed carries Florida's stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 of consideration, recorded through the clerk, with every party to the document answerable. Buyers see a different number from yours: after a sale, the property goes back to market value on the following January 1.

Selling with tax owed

You can list it, sell to a cash buyer, or catch up the tax first. The lien stays with the parcel, so it has to be cleared by closing in every case. For a rental or inherited home with several unpaid years, obtain a payoff letter first so the net figure on any offer is real.

If the house changed hands recently, the appraiser's record shows a reset value, and the fire assessment and utility bills still follow the parcel through the city. A buyer's lender will ask for current tax and utility status, so keep copies of the last bill and any payoff letter handy.

Rentals and inherited homes also raise a utility question: confirm who holds the city accounts and whether any city charges are past due. A cash buyer who accepts the house as is can close without showings or repairs, which helps when you need to settle a tax balance from the price. The payoffs still come out of the sale, so the title company needs them early.

A simple order of work keeps this tidy. First, ask the Leon County Tax Collector for a written payoff covering every open year. Second, ask the city utility office what is owed on the accounts tied to the address, including the fire assessment, trash and stormwater lines. Third, hand both figures to the title company so they appear on the settlement statement. Finally, confirm with the Leon County Property Appraiser that your homestead will drop off after the deed records, so a bill for next year does not arrive in your name.

If you owe nothing, closing is routine: the agent prorates the current year, records the deed and sends you the net. If you owe several years, the same steps apply, but the payoff grows each month after April 1, so the sooner you get a number, the smaller it will be. Ask for the figure in writing and note the date it is good through.

Frequently asked questions

What city millage applies to Tallahassee property?

The city's budget lists 4.4072 mills for fiscal year 2026. County, school and other levies add to it on the Leon County bill.

By what date must Leon County tax be paid?

Before April 1. Bills begin going out November 1, and a late bill picks up a delinquency fee, an advertising fee and 1.5 percent interest per month.

How much can I save by paying a Leon County bill early?

Four percent in November, three in December, two in January and one in February.

How large is the 2026 homestead exemption in Leon County?

Up to $51,411. The first $25,000 touches all taxes; the rest touches non-school taxes above $50,000. Filing closes March 1.

Why does so much Tallahassee property pay no tax?

Governments own over half the real property inside city limits, and it is exempt. The city bills a fire assessment and moves money from its utilities to cover services on those parcels.

Fort Lauderdale housing at a glance

About 188,677 people live in Fort Lauderdale, and just 54.1 percent of homes are owner occupied, so plenty of tax bills go to landlords. The median value of an owned home is $486,700, and 19.6 percent of residents are 65 or older. That senior share is why the low-income senior exemption below is worth a look. Waterfront houses and the condos beside the water are the parcels the appraiser studies most closely.

Which county office does what

The city does not value or bill property. Broward County does both. The appraiser handles valuation and exemption review (main line 954-357-6830, exemption help 954-357-5579, office at 1801 NW 49 Street, Suite PA1). The tax collector handles billing (954-357-4829).

The appraiser sends no bills, only notices. To record a deed, go to the county Recording Office at 115 S. Andrews Avenue, Room 114 (954-831-4000).

Dates that matter each year

State timing governs, and Broward adds its own exemption filing periods.

WhenWhat happens
January 1Value and residency are measured
March 1On-time exemption filing ends
AugustTRIM notice mailed

NovemberBills issued, top discount begins

After November the early-pay discount drops one point each month.

Filing for homestead in Broward

The on-time period for the 2027 roll closes March 1, 2027. It is open to people who owned the home and made it their permanent residence after January 1, 2026. If you miss it, late filing runs to September 20, 2027, and the appraiser cites section 196.011(8) to explain that nothing, good cause included, extends that date.

Bring Florida identification, meaning a voter registration or a power or water bill in an owner's name. For trust ownership, add a notarized certificate of trust or the full instrument. File online at bcpa.net/onlinehomestead.asp, or send paper forms by email, fax or mail.

What the basic exemption saves

For 2026 the appraiser puts the saving at $673 to $1,020 per qualifying home worth $75,000 or more. The spread comes from different city millage rates. State materials describe a $50,000 maximum, where the first $25,000 applies to school taxes and the rest to other levies.

Homestead assessed value is capped at the lesser of 3 percent and inflation, and the state chart gives 2.7 percent for 2026. Non-homestead parcels have a 10 percent ceiling. Each cap restarts at sale, so a buyer's first bill can look nothing like yours.

Other exemptions

Each has its own paperwork, and the appraiser welcomes calls at 954-357-6830.

  • Low-income seniors: age 65 on January 1, with homestead and household income below the printed cap of $38,686, adjusted yearly. Filing runs January 1 to March 1.
  • $5,000 breaks for disability, blindness and widowed owners.
  • A $5,000 disability break for service members, and a full exemption for total and permanent service-connected disability.
  • A granny flat exemption for a permitted addition housing a parent or grandparent aged 62 or older, capped at 20 percent of homestead value.
  • Historic property exemptions.

Challenging a value

Have your TRIM notice and a copy of your property record in hand, then call first, since clerical errors often get fixed informally. If that fails, file a petition with the clerk during the 25 days after the August notice. If you disagree with the answer, write down what you were told and by whom before moving on. A denied exemption goes before the Value Adjustment Board instead, on a 30 day clock from the date of the denial letter.

Board staff work from 1801 NW 49th Street (954-357-7205 or 954-357-5444) and take disputes over exemptions, classifications and valuations.

Before you list the house

  • Look up the parcel on the property appraiser's website and test each exemption shown against how you actually use the house.
  • If a storm left the house uninhabitable for 30 days or more, the appraiser accepts a catastrophic structural damage report.
  • Decide whether this year's bill gets paid now or from closing proceeds.
  • Report any rental use accurately, since renting can end homestead.
  • Ask the collector how a deferral or installment plan behaves if you sell.

Landlords selling a rental should ask the appraiser about rental and business property rules alongside the homestead ones.

Postponing or splitting the bill

Two routes exist. Deferral uses Form DR-570, filed by March 31, and postpones the portion above 5 percent of household income, all of it when income is under $10,000. For permanent residents 65 or older the threshold is 3 percent. Installments require an application to the collector by May 1.

Either way, the August notice previews what is coming. If you plan to sell, tell the collector before you list, because a deferral or installment plan may need to be settled at closing. Ask for the exact payoff in writing, and hand it to your title agent so the number on the settlement statement matches.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

A sale from start to finish

Taxes run through every stage of a sale, so it helps to know the order. First, look up your parcel and read the exemptions and value shown. Second, check the amount due and whether the lender pays it from escrow. Third, once you have a contract, the title agent orders payoffs for the mortgage and any tax balance.

Fourth, the agent prepares a settlement statement that splits the year's tax between you and the buyer. Review it a few days ahead and ask about any line you do not recognize. Last, at closing you sign the deed, the agent pays the balances and the deed is recorded. A sale to a cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting steps, which can shorten that timeline when a tax date or other deadline is near.

What stays and what goes at sale

Broward's appraiser tells buyers not to assume the seller's tax continues, because a change of ownership resets assessed value to full market value. Exemptions stay behind, and the buyer applies anew. What you can carry is accumulated Save Our Homes savings, through portability to a new Florida homestead begun within a three year window. The appraiser offers a portability estimator. The exemption itself never moves.

The closing agent prorates the year's tax between you and the buyer. The appraiser also runs a free Owner Alert that notifies you when a document changing ownership of your property reaches its office.

On closing day, bring photo ID and your most recent tax bill. The title agent pays any balance from your proceeds and gives you a final statement, which is worth keeping with your tax records for the year of sale.

Frequently asked questions

When is a Fort Lauderdale tax bill due?

Bills are issued in November, and a balance still open on April 1 turns delinquent. The largest discount rewards November payment and fades by February.

Where does a Fort Lauderdale homeowner apply for homestead?

With the Broward appraiser, online or on paper. The on-time deadline is March 1, and 2027 late filings stop September 20, 2027.

Does the city assess my house?

No. Broward's appraiser values it and Broward's collector bills it. The city is only one of the taxing bodies on the bill.

Can I contest a Fort Lauderdale assessment?

Yes. Petition the clerk during the 25 days after the August notice, or use the Value Adjustment Board for a denied exemption. A call to the appraiser first often resolves errors.

Can renting out the house cost me the exemption?

It can. The exemption rests on permanent residence, so full-time rental use may end eligibility. Report changes in use to the appraiser.

Selling in Gainesville: the basics

Gainesville has 151,275 residents and is both the Alachua County seat and its biggest city. The University of Florida and Santa Fe College bring so many students that median age is 26.4, which means buyers tend to be a blend of owner-occupants and investors. The rest of this page covers what a seller needs to know about the tax bill.

Who bills a Gainesville tax bill

Billing comes from Alachua County, not the city. The county property appraiser handles value and exemptions, the tax collector handles mailing and collection, and the city is just one of the bodies whose rates appear on the bill.

  • Tax collector: phone (352) 374-5236 if no bill arrives in November. Delinquent-tax payment questions go to its Tax Operations Department at (352) 264-6968.
  • Property appraiser: prepares the tax roll and decides homestead, disability, widow and agricultural exemptions. Its tangible division answers at (352) 374-5234.
  • City commission: sets the city millage as part of its annual budget.
  • County commission: sets county millage and certain non-ad valorem assessments.

Non-ad valorem charges on a bill can include mandatory refuse collection, rural collection center, solid waste management, paving, water extension, fire, storm water and PACE assessments. Lower-income owners may be excused from some of them through the county social services office at (352) 264-6750.

If you have moved or sold recently, make sure the bill is going to the right person. Send the appraiser your new mailing address, and tell your buyer or closing agent which tax year's bill is still outstanding. A bill that lands in an old mailbox still carries the same due dates.

City millage rate

The city's rate for fiscal year 2027 is 6.7297 mills, meaning $6.7297 per $1,000 of taxable value. Its rolled-back rate is 6.3839, and the two-thirds vote maximum is 7.0223.

Those numbers cover the city alone. Your parcel also carries lines from the county, the school board and the water district, and the TRIM notice and September hearings can still shift the final figures. The November bill shows what was set, and the tax collector can confirm it.

Due dates and the early-payment discount

Expect your statement in the mailbox by the first of November. You can pay the full amount any time through March 31, and delinquency begins April 1. What you save for paying early shrinks every month.

If a lender escrows for you, it asks for the bill itself and your copy is informational. It has to pay within the 4 percent window. Once a loan is paid off, the lender is supposed to remove your account from its list, so confirm that the bill now comes to you if you recently cleared a mortgage.

Installment plan

Accounts whose tax last year topped $100 can split this year's bill into four payments through the county tax collector. You must sign up by April 30.

  • June 30: first payment, with a 6 percent reduction.
  • September 30: second payment, 4.5 percent reduction.
  • December 31: third payment, 3 percent reduction.
  • March 31: final payment at full price.

Payments one and two are each a quarter of the previous year's tax. Payments three and four divide whatever is left of the real liability. If the June payment is skipped, you are out for the year and a regular November bill comes. When a due date lands on a weekend or holiday, it moves to the next business day.

Unpaid taxes

Any real estate tax still open on April 1 draws a minimum 3 percent charge. During May each late parcel is advertised in a local paper for three weeks, and the cost is added to what you owe. The collector then holds an online certificate sale at lienhub.com on or before June 1.

Bidding starts at 18 percent and runs downward. The certificate pays its holder at least 5 percent unless the winning bid is zero, and it is a first lien that lasts seven years. Once two years run from the delinquency, the holder may request a tax deed, and the parcel then goes to public auction. You clear the lien by paying the collector.

Late taxes can be paid with cash, check, money order, debit card (minimum $2.50 fee), e-check ($1.00) or credit card and PayPal (2.5 percent fee). What you owe depends on the day the office receives the money.

Rental and business equipment

If you run a business or rent out a home, the furniture, fixtures and equipment there are taxed as tangible personal property, and so are structural additions to mobile homes. The Alachua County Property Appraiser values these items each January 1, based on a return that the owner files. File between January 1 and April 1 and you earn an exemption of up to $25,000; a late or missing return brings penalties and forfeits it.

Unpaid personal property tax is late on April 1, when a $10 fee and 1.5 percent monthly interest begin. On May 1 the collector adds a collection fee of 20 percent of the gross tax, and a warrant adds a $50 legal fee. Call the tangible division at (352) 374-5234.

Homestead and deferral

Homestead takes up to $50,000 off taxable value. File with the property appraiser by March 1, and remember the home must be your permanent residence. A statutory cap on assessed value growth, shown as 2.7 percent for 2026 on the state chart, protects owners, though a sale resets the next owner to just value.

The tax collector also offers a deferral. It is secured by a lien, carries interest capped at 7 percent a year, requires that the primary mortgage not exceed 70 percent of assessed value, and calls for proof of insurance. A change of ownership makes the whole deferred amount payable, so the closing agent must pay it.

Before you sell

Start by ordering a payoff from the Alachua County Tax Collector, and add any deferral balance to it. Your closing agent pays everything out of your proceeds. Tangible tax on a business or rental is prorated between buyer and seller at closing, and a lien for that tax survives a sale, so owners of rentals should confirm no personal property bill is open.

The tax year is January to December and the bill arrives in November. A spring closing may therefore still involve a bill you must settle. Cash buyers often agree to short timelines, which helps when April 1 delinquency is close.

Keep the paperwork in order. Pull your parcel record, confirm who receives the tax bill, request the payoff, and ask the title agent for a draft settlement statement before closing day. Check that each tax line matches the collector's number. If you rent the home, also gather the lease and any records of furniture or appliances left for tenants, since the appraiser may ask about them.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Gainesville millage rate?

The city's rate for fiscal year 2027 is 6.7297 mills. County, school and water district lines are added on top, and the final rates appear on your November bill or from the Alachua County Tax Collector.

Who collects Gainesville property tax?

The Alachua County Tax Collector. If you do not get a November bill, call (352) 374-5236.

When is Alachua County property tax late?

After March 31. Taxes become delinquent April 1, and a 3 percent minimum charge is added.

When can I apply for the Gainesville installment plan?

Sign-up closes April 30 each year, and the first payment is due June 30. The accounts must have owed more than $100 the year before.

Does a sale end my homestead deferral?

The deferral becomes due, with interest, when ownership changes. The closing agent should pay the balance from your proceeds.

The age of the housing stock

West Palm Beach began as a winter refuge for northerners, and its housing shows the layers. The 1920s brought platted neighborhoods and a rush of cottages and bungalows. After World War II, returning soldiers built postwar and midcentury infill that fills several neighborhoods today.

A listing here can be a 1920s bungalow, a midcentury ranch or a newer place near the western preserve, and each reaches the tax roll with a different value history. Read the parcel record before you trust any citywide figure, and pull the property control number so you can look up the exact levies, exemptions and taxable value for that address.

Does a historic district limit what you can do before selling?

It can, if the house sits inside one. The city counts 17 historic districts, nine of them on the National Register of Historic Places, plus more than 45 individually designated sites.

  • Exterior changes to a designated property are reviewed by city staff or the Historic Preservation Board, depending on scope.
  • Historic approval has to come before any permit is issued for the work.
  • Routine upkeep that needs no permit, such as painting or minor exterior repair, skips extra review.

The planner on call at (561) 822-1461 can say whether an address is designated. A seller planning a pre-listing addition should ask that question first, because work done without approval is a problem the buyer inherits.

Tax break for restoring a historic home

A city program in effect since February 14, 1994 exempts up to 100 percent of the added assessed value that comes from renovating a designated historic property. The exemption runs for ten years and covers interior or exterior work.

The city's own illustration is a house assessed at $250,000 whose new kitchen, bedroom suite and porch lift taxable value to $290,000. The $40,000 difference is then exempt from part of the ad valorem tax for the decade. The plans need Historic Preservation Board approval before work begins, and construction has to finish within two years of that approval, following the Secretary of the Interior's rehabilitation standards.

Income-producing buildings such as rentals can instead look at a 20 percent federal tax credit on rehabilitation costs, administered through the National Park Service. If you are selling a renovated historic house, mention an active exemption in the listing, and if you are buying one, ask about it.

Who bills a West Palm Beach parcel?

The Palm Beach County Property Appraiser values the parcel, and the Palm Beach County Tax Collector sends the bill. The city adds only its own levy. The collector mails more than 600,000 bills, wrapping up by November 1, and spreads the proceeds across county and city government, schools, fire districts, libraries, parks, children's services and the healthcare district.

Notices follow the mailing address in the appraiser's file. After you sell or move, update it, or file the collector's Property Sold Form so the next bill finds the buyer.

Millage rates for the city

The appraiser's rate page lists every levy in one place. A mill is one dollar of tax per thousand dollars of taxable value.

Payment window and discounts

Payment opens November 1 and closes March 31. The discount steps down from 4 percent in November to 3, 2 and 1 percent, then disappears in March.

  • Delinquent bills cannot be paid online.
  • A payment counts for a month only if it arrives by that month's last working day, since a postmark is not proof.
  • Weekend or holiday deadlines slide forward.

The collector's important dates page helps when a closing falls close to a month end.

If the bill goes unpaid past March

The collector holds a certificate sale 60 days after delinquency or on June 1, whichever is later (s. 197.402). A certificate is an investor's first lien. Unsold ones go to the county and grow at 1.5 percent a month. Redemption needs the tax, interest, advertising costs and a $6.25 fee, and two years of waiting lets the holder seek a tax deed. The clerk runs that auction, and the high bidder pays in full within 24 hours.

For a homeowner in this spot, the practical step is to call the collector before the sale and ask for a redemption figure. Selling the house and paying the lien from the proceeds is cleaner than letting a deed process start.

How to dispute a value

Call the appraiser first at 561.355.3230 for an informal review, then file with the Value Adjustment Board if needed. Talking to staff does not pause the clock.

The board has five seats: two county commissioners, one school board member and two citizens. Special magistrates hear valuation, portability, deferral and change of ownership disputes and recommend rulings. The clerk's office runs the process separately from the appraiser.

  • The petition is due within 25 days of the TRIM mailing each year.
  • The fee can be up to $20.
  • Single parcels file online through the clerk's portal. Contiguous parcels go by mail or in person.
  • Mail to PO Box 4036, West Palm Beach, FL 33402, or deliver to 301 North Olive Avenue, Room 206.
  • A deficient petition gets a Clerk's Notice and 10 calendar days to cure.

Before closing

Ask the title agent for a payoff letter that runs through the closing date, and confirm no certificate sits on the parcel. The collector posts a delinquent list and a RealAuction search for county-held certificates.

  • A sale ends your homestead, and the following January 1 sets the buyer's assessment at just value.
  • If you buy another Florida home, ask the appraiser about portability and its three-year window.
  • Deed stamps are 70 cents per $100 here, and the contract says who pays.

The collector's page also flags a statewide amendment, so ask which changes touch your parcel. A cash buyer skips lender escrow questions, but the payoff and certificate check still apply.

Reading the sample bill

The collector's sample bill labels the property control number, owners, situs address, exemptions, assessed, exempt and taxable values, and the amount due per discount month, plus a QR code for payment. Taxable value times each authority's millage gives the ad valorem charge, and non-ad valorem items such as solid waste fees are added. Use that layout to check a payoff statement line by line.

Frequently asked questions

What is the West Palm Beach city millage rate?

8.1308 mills for 2025 and a proposed 8.1308 for 2026, plus a debt service line. Confirm the certified number with the tax collector.

How many historic districts does West Palm Beach have?

The city counts 17, nine of them on the National Register, plus more than 45 individually designated sites.

How long does the historic renovation exemption last?

Ten years, and it covers up to 100 percent of the assessed value added by approved work on a designated property.

When does a West Palm Beach bill turn delinquent?

April 1, and after that it cannot be paid online.

Who holds the Palm Beach County tax deed sale?

The Clerk and Comptroller runs it, and the high bidder pays in full within 24 hours.

Where the Boca Raton tax bill comes from

A single bill arrives from the Palm Beach County Tax Collector, and the Property Appraiser sets the value. The city itself levies only a slice: the city's August 2026 Property Taxes Explained brochure shows eight taxing authorities on a Boca Raton bill, with 21.67 percent of the tax going to the city.

Bills are mailed by November 1, more than 600,000 of them, to the address the Property Appraiser has on file. Taxes are payable from November 1 through March 31.

  • Value, exemptions and mailing address: Palm Beach County Property Appraiser, (561) 355-2866.
  • Bills, delinquent tax, installment plan, deferral and tax certificates: Palm Beach County Tax Collector, delinquent line (561) 355-2264.
  • City levy and fire assessment: City of Boca Raton, 201 West Palmetto Park Road.

Taxing authorities and rates

Eight authorities appear: the Palm Beach County School Board, Palm Beach County operating and debt, Boca Raton operating and debt, the Health Care District, the Greater Boca Raton Beach and Park District, the Children's Services Council, the South Florida Water Management District and the Florida Inland Navigational District.

The city's own rate over time

The city's operating rate sat near 3.45 mills in 2018 and is shown at 3.6476 mills for both 2026 and 2027, while a separate debt service rate fell from 0.2245 to 0.0163 over the same stretch. Combined, the city's total millage moved only between 3.6788 and 3.6639 across the ten years charted. The 2027 column is the city's proposed figure, so read it as a plan, not a final bill.

Because the city's slice has held steady, larger swings in a Boca Raton bill come from the school board and county lines.

Fire protection is billed as a non-ad valorem assessment, printed at $170.00, which sits on the bill beside the millage. Unincorporated Palm Beach County instead pays a fire MSTU based on assessed value.

What the city levy pays for

The city's operating budget is $723,811,900, with 1,951 full time equivalent employees, 224 police officers and 269 firefighters working from 8 fire stations. It handles 47,161 police calls and 18,872 fire and rescue calls a year and maintains 49 parks covering 1,072.03 acres. Police and fire cost $172.3 million to run, against proposed property taxes of $150.2 million.

If a buyer asks why a Boca Raton bill looks the way it does, the City's Property Taxes Explained brochure shows each authority's share of the $693,362,086 that residents pay each year. The School Board takes 37.18 percent and Palm Beach County operating and debt takes 26.74 percent.

Due dates and discounts

Pay any time from November through March. April starts delinquency, and March carries no discount.

The early payment ladder from the Palm Beach County Tax Collector is 4 percent off in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February. Gross tax is due March 31, and when that date falls on a weekend or holiday it slides to the next business day.

Delinquent tax cannot be paid online, and a postmark stops counting as proof of payment. To count for a given month, payment must arrive by that month's last working day. The delinquent line will confirm what you owe.

Exemptions and caps for Boca Raton homes

File for homestead with the Palm Beach County Property Appraiser by March 1. The house has to be your permanent home as of January 1.

On a typical Boca Raton bill the homestead exemption is $50,000 against most levies but only $25,000 against school district tax, because the second $25,000 never applies to school taxes. Amendment 1 is what created the double exemption for every levy except school.

  • Save Our Homes keeps assessed value from rising faster than 3 percent or CPI each year, whichever is lower, and Florida's chart prints 2.7 percent for 2026.
  • Portability lets you carry that benefit to a new homestead inside three years.
  • After a sale, the next owner is assessed at full just value the following January.
  • Seniors, disabled ex-servicemembers and deployed servicemembers have their own exemptions under state law and local ordinance.
