Market context for sellers

Boca Raton has 101,582 residents in about 29 square miles of land. Owners live in 65.7 percent of homes, and the median home value is $722,700. Median gross rent is $2,508 and median household income is $106,273. Residents 65 and over are 24.6 percent of the population, so many sellers are retirees downsizing or heirs settling an estate. The city counts 49,050 dwelling units and an assessed value of $42.7 billion.

At these values, the tax adjustments at closing are large. Florida's deed stamp tax, 70 cents per $100 of price outside Miami-Dade, falls on every party to the deed, and the closing statement should divide the year's tax and any fire assessment.

If you fall behind on tax

Call the Tax Collector before delinquency begins in April. Once a bill is delinquent it can no longer be paid on the online portal, and a late payment is judged by when it arrives, not its postmark. When you call, have the bill number from the Property Control Number box on the notice. Both an installment plan and a homestead tax deferral are options.

State deadlines: Form DR-570 for deferral by March 31, and installment applications by May 1 of the assessment year. Certificates go up for sale by June 1. After two years the holder can seek a tax deed, and on homestead property the opening bid on the deed includes half the assessed value.

A house with a certificate can still be sold, and the payoff comes out of proceeds at closing. Because delinquent balances change month to month, get the figure in writing from the Tax Collector.

Getting ready to sell

This order works for most Boca Raton sellers.

  1. Open your Property Appraiser record and verify the owner name, mailing address and exemptions.
  2. Ask the Tax Collector what is owed and whether a discount month is still running.
  3. Find the fire assessment on the bill so you can explain it to a buyer.
  4. Send the numbers to your title company early, so the closing statement divides the year correctly.

Selling for cash skips the lender and the appraisal, but the tax proration, the deed stamp tax and any lien payoff still apply.

Does the City of Boca Raton send its own tax bill?

No. The Palm Beach County Tax Collector sends one bill that includes the city and seven other taxing authorities.

What is the Boca Raton millage rate?

It depends on the location. The city's sample prints 3.6639 mills for the city operating and debt levy and a total of 16.9090, labeled as the 2026-27 proposed figure. Check your parcel's final rate with the Property Appraiser.

When do Boca Raton property taxes become delinquent?

April 1. Gross tax is due March 31, and delinquent tax cannot be paid online.

Which office answers questions about a Boca Raton exemption?

The Palm Beach County Property Appraiser, at (561) 355-2866. Applications are due on March 1.

Does the buyer inherit my Save Our Homes cap?

No. A change of ownership resets assessed value to just value the following January 1, with limited exceptions such as certain spousal transfers.

Where Ocala owners take tax questions

Ocala sits in Marion County, so the county appraiser sets its values and the county collector mails the bills. Millage comes from several boards, including the City of Ocala, the county commission and the school board.

You can visit the appraiser at 501 SE 25th Avenue in Ocala, with or without an appointment. Online, the office runs a homestead e-file, a tax estimator and a mortgage estimate letter, and links out to the TRIM notice and the value adjustment board.

Housing in Ocala

The city had 71,753 residents in 2025, a gain of 12.7 percent over 2020, spread over 47.26 square miles. The median owner-occupied value is $241,400 and median gross rent is $1,359. Only 52.1 percent of homes are owner-occupied, so rental parcels are common. Rented homes cannot hold a homestead exemption, so a landlord selling an Ocala rental should expect the buyer's bill to follow the non-homestead rules.

Owner costs run $1,598 a month with a mortgage and $573 without one, a gap worth showing a first-time buyer.

How a tax bill is built

The appraiser multiplies value after exemptions by the millage the taxing bodies set, then certifies the roll for collection. Dates below follow the state schedule.

March 1Exemption applications close

April 1Unpaid bills turn delinquent

Buyers can try the appraiser's estimator for a rough figure. Their value restarts after the sale, so your old bill is a poor guide.

Online tools for sellers

You can handle most paperwork from home. The appraiser's website points to these tools:

  • Property search, a map tool and a sales search for checking what nearby parcels went for.
  • A homestead exemption e-file and a property tax estimator.
  • A mortgage estimate letter, which lenders and buyers sometimes request.
  • A mailing address change form, handy if you move out ahead of closing.
  • A form to report property damage, and a separate link to report homestead fraud.
  • Pages for tangible personal property: an e-filed return, an extension request and forms.

Before you list an Ocala home, run the sales search for your street and print the results. Nearby sales answer the buyer who asks why your price differs from the assessed value. The office also posts important dates, a taxpayer's bill of rights and frequently asked questions.

Landlords and heirs

Many Ocala sellers are investors or heirs, not homestead owners. A non-homestead parcel is limited to 10 percent growth a year, and that limit ends at sale.

Heirs have extra steps. A personal representative's deed under a probated will carries no stamp tax, but estate planning transfers get no blanket exemption. Florida requires no estate tax return for deaths after 2004.

  • Summary administration fits a non-exempt estate of $150,000 or less, or a death more than two years back.

Limited-income seniors may defer part of a homestead bill, so ask the collector how a deferral plays out in a sale before you take an offer.

Before you take an offer

Open the parcel record on the appraiser's site and read the owner name, mailing address and exemptions. A wrong name or address delays notices, and an exemption still on a house you rented out will raise questions with the buyer's lender.

Then ask the collector to confirm every year is paid. Bills follow the calendar year, so a summer sale has no mailed bill yet and the title company estimates it. A house once rented furnished may owe tangible personal property tax on the furniture and equipment, with a return due by April 1.

  • Ask the title company for a tax proration worksheet early.
  • Gather any denial letters or value notices still in dispute.
  • Tell the buyer which taxing bodies appear on the bill, including the City of Ocala.

Discounts and ways to pay

November payments get 4 percent off, followed by 3, 2 and 1 percent through February. Even if no bill arrives, the owner has to find the amount and pay before April 1.

If paying in one lump is hard, ask the collector about installments (apply by May 1) or a partial payment before delinquency. Seniors with limited income can use Form DR-570 by March 31 to defer part of a homestead bill.

Homestead and the assessment cap

To qualify for the exemption of up to $50,000, the house must be your permanent residence on January 1, and the application is due March 1. Yearly growth in assessed value was capped at 2.7 percent for 2026.

A sale resets the next assessment to just value, with exceptions for spouse transfers and certain transfers on death. An owner buying again in Florida can ask the appraiser about carrying savings to the new home through portability.

A short pre-listing checklist

These are general steps any seller can take. Print your parcel record and last tax statement. Write down who holds any mortgage and request a payoff letter. List every exemption you have on file so you can tell the buyer and the title agent what will drop off. Keep the dates of any notice you receive, and note which deadline each one starts. Finally, decide who in your household will sign documents and make sure that person's name matches the deed exactly.

Doing this before the first showing means a contract can move quickly, and it gives you a clear answer when a buyer asks about taxes.

What happens at an Ocala closing

At the table, the title company confirms payoffs, splits the current year's tax between you and the buyer, and has you sign the deed, which the clerk then records. Ask for the settlement statement a day early so any tax line you cannot place can be explained.

With cash there is no lender appraisal or underwriting, so the calendar shortens. Tax and title chores are unchanged: leftover balances come out of your proceeds and recorded liens get released before title passes.

Deed taxes, fees and back taxes

A deed for an Ocala property is taxed at the statewide 70 cents per $100 of consideration (section 201.02). Everyone on the deed stays liable, and the clerk takes payment. Clerk recording charges start at $5.00 for the first page (section 28.24).

  • Warranty, special warranty and quit claim deeds are taxable.
  • Certain spousal and divorce deeds for the marital home are exempt.

Back taxes lead to certificates sold by June 1 and, later, a possible deed sale. Settle the account with the collector before listing, and have the title company pull a payoff so closing figures are firm.

Frequently asked questions

Which county taxes a home in Ocala?

Marion County, Florida. The county's appraiser values the home and its collector bills it, using millage from several bodies that includes the City of Ocala.

What is Ocala's median home value?

$241,400. Median rent is $1,359, and 52.1 percent of units have owners living in them.

Where can an Ocala owner visit the appraiser?

At 501 SE 25th Avenue in Ocala. Walk-ins and appointments are both welcome, and the phone number is (352) 368-8300.

Can an Ocala rental property have homestead?

No. Homestead is lost if the unit is rented, so a rental is assessed without the exemption and the owner's cap does not transfer to a buyer.

Is the Ocala tax bill reset when the house sells?

Yes. A transfer of title sends the next assessment to just value, so a buyer cannot count on the seller's bill.

One bill for city residents

The City of Sarasota doesn't mail its own tax bill. A house inside city limits gets a single notice from the county tax collector, with the city listed as one of several taxing bodies. The county appraiser's value is the starting point for every line.

Expect city, county, school board and district charges to share the page with non-ad valorem items for services like fire protection and trash. Start with the appraiser's property search to find your parcel, then open the collector's account page to see what has been billed. For the full county calendar, read the county tax guide. Amendment 3 and your future bill

The ballot summary raises the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, then indexes it. It also cuts the yearly cap on non-homestead assessment growth from 10 percent to 5 percent.

New arrivals are treated differently. Anyone who is not a Florida resident on December 31, 2026 gets the current exemption first and the larger one from the fifth year. Local governments would also be limited to listed uses of property tax revenue, including public safety, schools, infrastructure and debt service. The effective date is January 1, 2027.

Locally, the 2026 notice is payable as issued, and the changes reach the 2027 bill. School taxes and non-ad valorem charges stay. If you're pricing a house, ask the appraiser what the changes mean for your parcel.

Proof needed for homestead

Expect the appraiser to ask for proof of ownership, proof of residency and facts about any prior home. You must be a Florida resident living in the house on January 1, and March 1 is the timely application date.

A recorded deed, tax bill or TRIM notice will serve as ownership proof. For residency, bring a Florida license or ID with the home address, and at least one of voter registration, vehicle registration or a recorded declaration of domicile. A second route uses two items from a different list: a W-2 or paystub, children's school registration, a federal tax return, or utility and bank records. If you still own your old home, show that its exemption was cancelled. If you sold it, show the sale date.

  • Both spouses supply their details.
  • Each applicant needs a Social Security number.
  • A permanent resident who is not a citizen shows a green card.

The Save Our Homes cap at a sale

For you, the cap ends at closing. It limits yearly assessed growth to 3 percent or CPI, whichever is lower, and a sale lets the appraiser reset the parcel to just value the next January 1.

The state's cap chart, revised in January 2026, shows 3.0 percent for 2024, 2.9 percent for 2025 and 2.7 percent for 2026. A family that has held a Sarasota home for decades may carry a wide gap between assessed and market value. The buyer starts with none of it.

Portability cushions the loss for the seller. Establish a new Florida homestead within three years of January 1 of the year you left the old one, and file DR-501T with the DR-501 by March 1. The transferred amount is the lesser of $500,000 or the old home's just-minus-assessed gap, and 2026 amendments first apply to the 2027 roll.

Exemptions that don't require living there

Four $5,000 exemptions can be claimed on any one Florida property a permanent resident owns: widow or widower, total and permanent disability, blindness, and disabled veteran at 10 percent or higher.

Other benefits need homestead. Seniors of limited means may qualify for an added exemption, with income papers due June 1. A veteran with a total and permanent service-connected disability may have homestead tax waived, and the benefit can pass to a surviving spouse.

Selling with back taxes

The buyer answers to the collector for the entire bill, whenever the purchase happens. Your share appears on the settlement statement as a credit, not as a payment to the collector. A bill that reaches a former owner goes back to the new owner or to the collector. At the clerk's counter, the deed carries stamp tax of $0.70 per $100, rounded up. A long delinquency can lead to the process on our tax deed page.

A workable order: request the balance, give it to the title agent, review the payoff on the closing statement, and keep the receipt. If closing slips by a few weeks, ask for the payoff to be refreshed, since late-year figures can change.

Paperwork for disability and widow exemptions

Each claim has its own proof. Gather it before March 1 so a first-time filing isn't held up.

  • Widow or widower: an application, and possibly a copy of the death certificate. Remarriage ends the exemption.
  • Total and permanent disability: a Florida physician's certification on form DR-416, or a certificate from the federal VA.
  • Blindness: a certificate from the state Division of Blind Services, the VA or the Social Security Administration, or a physician or optometrist form.
  • Disabled veteran: a letter, certificate or ID card from the government showing the rating.
  • Wheelchair or legally blind homestead exemption: two unrelated Florida physicians on DR-416, plus a Statement of Gross Income on DR-501A.

The income test for that last exemption counts VA benefits and Social Security.

Complaints about value or rates

Value goes first to the appraiser and then to the Value Adjustment Board, within 25 days of the TRIM mailing. Rates go to the budget hearings listed on the notice.

The board decides value, classification and exemption questions only. Florida's calendar puts tentative budget hearings in September and October and final hearings after that. A hearing is where a rate complaint belongs, so mark the date when the notice arrives. Bring any comparable sales or repair estimates with you to a value hearing, and ask the appraiser to review them before the petition deadline.

Handling a tax problem in order

Match each question to the office that owns it: value and exemptions to the appraiser, the bill to the collector, recorded paper to the clerk.

  • Open your parcel on the appraiser's search, then use the button near the top of the record to view the TRIM.
  • Check that exemptions survived any name or address change.
  • Look for a prior-year balance on the collector's account page.
  • Search the clerk's Official Records for liens.
  • Join the clerk's fraud alerts for the owner's name.

Work through the list before you list the house. A buyer's title search will find any open item anyway, so it's cheaper to learn about it first.

Does the City of Sarasota collect property tax itself?

No. The county tax collector bills for every taxing body inside the city, so you pay one notice.

What is the city millage rate?

The city sets its own rate, which is one line on your bill. Read your TRIM notice or ask the city or appraiser for the current figure.

When must I apply for homestead?

By March 1, having lived in the house as your permanent home on January 1. Late filings are still reviewed.

Does the Save Our Homes cap pass to a buyer?

No. A sale resets assessed value to just value the next January 1, though portability may carry part of the benefit to your next Florida home.

Can I sell with unpaid taxes?

Yes, and the balance is normally settled from the proceeds at closing after the title agent confirms the amount.

Who sends the Pensacola tax bill

The envelope for a Pensacola address is mailed by the Escambia County tax collector, using a value supplied by the county property appraiser. Inside the city limits, one parcel can answer to several taxing bodies at once.

Among the bodies the collector bills for are the school board, the county commission, the City of Pensacola, the Town of Century, the Sheriff, the Downtown Improvement Board and the Northwest Florida Water Management District. The appraiser has no say over budgets, tax rates or special assessments. Rate complaints belong with whichever taxing body set the rate. Value or exemption questions go to escpa.org.

Pensacola in brief for sellers

The city counted 54,312 residents in 2020, and household income has a median of $72,699 for 2019 to 2023. Naval Air Station Pensacola brings a steady flow of newcomers on military orders, which keeps a buyer pool coming even in slow months.

Location inside the city moves the bill. On the appraiser's millage page the Downtown Improvement Board stands as its own authority, and Pensacola Beach has a separate total. Look at the parcel record before pricing the house, since a Beach address and a downtown address are taxed differently.

Payment dates and discounts

Bills go out in November. For 2026 bills the collector shows a 4 percent discount through December 2, 2026, then 3 percent for the rest of that month, 2 percent in January 2027 and 1 percent in February 2027. The full amount is due in March 2027, and anything unpaid is delinquent on April 1, 2027.

The collector's notice on Amendment 3 says voters approved it on November 3, 2026. The vote leaves the 2026 bill alone, and new homestead exemption amounts begin with the 2027 tax year.

Escambia also offers a quarterly plan to taxpayers whose prior year taxes topped $100 and who have no mortgage escrow. Sign up by April 30 of the year you want to use it.

Exemptions a Pensacola homeowner can claim

Homestead is first on the list. The appraiser wants the application in before March 1. You qualify if you hold title, live in the home in good faith and make it your permanent home on January 1.

  • Homestead: $25,000 off every levy, plus up to $25,000 more on assessed value over $50,000 for levies other than school taxes.
  • Senior add-on: owners 65 by January 1 whose household adjusted gross income is under the yearly cap, printed as $38,686 for 2026. The county's $50,000 covers county taxes only, and a separate City of Pensacola $50,000 covers city taxes only.
  • Widow or widower: $5,000, supported by a death certificate.
  • Disability or blindness: $5,000, with proof from Social Security or a Florida physician.

Who pays in the year of the sale

Your buyer's first bill may look nothing like yours. After a sale the assessment is reset to market value, so an asking price pitched around your old tax figure can mislead. Point buyers to the appraiser's record instead.

  • Look up the deed history in the clerk's Official Records.

Where a Pensacola deed is recorded

Escambia's clerk of court maintains the Official Records; search them at escambiaclerk.com. Deed stamps run at seventy cents per $100 of price in every Florida county but Miami-Dade, and the Department of Revenue says the clerk collects the tax when a deed is recorded.

Before you list, gather four things: your latest bill, the exemption confirmation from the appraiser, the deed as recorded and any letter from the collector about open years. Having them in one folder lets the title agent start on day one.

Planning a fast sale, with an agent or to a cash buyer? Call the collector early. A written payoff holds for a stated date only, so you may need a fresh one if closing slips. Without a lender involved there is no loan review, but the title company still checks every tax year on the parcel.

Questions to ask the collector

A short list helps. Which years are paid? Is any certificate outstanding? What is the payoff if closing happens on a date you name? Are any special district charges on the parcel, and do they change with the sale? Write down the answers and the date, and keep the reply with your closing documents. If the answers are unclear, ask for them in writing and ask who at the office can confirm a figure for your closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Does the city or the county send the Pensacola bill?

The county does. Escambia's tax collector issues it, and the City of Pensacola is one of several lines on it, next to the county, the school district and districts such as the Downtown Improvement Board.

They start with the November bill at 4 percent and step down monthly to 1 percent in February. For 2026 bills the collector shows 4 percent through December 2, 2026, with delinquency on April 1, 2027.

Yes, if last year's tax was over $100 and you have no escrow account. Apply by April 30; payments fall on June 30, September 30, December 31 and March 31.

What does the senior exemption give in Pensacola?

It gives $50,000 off county taxes and a separate $50,000 off city taxes for owners past 65 under the income cap. The appraiser prints the 2026 cap as $38,686, with applications closing March 1.

Will a Pensacola sale change the taxable value?

Yes. A sale counts as a change of ownership, so the parcel is reassessed at market value and the new owner must apply for their own homestead before the Save Our Homes limit starts again.

Who bills Port St. Lucie property tax

Port St. Lucie lies in St. Lucie County. Three county offices touch your house. The Property Appraiser sets its value, the Tax Collector mails and collects the bill, and the Clerk of Court files your deed. The city adds only its own lines.

The appraiser (paslc.gov) has two offices: Fort Pierce at 2300 Virginia Avenue and Saint Lucie West at 250 NW Country Club Drive. The phone for both is 772-462-1000. The city millage rate

The city rate is 4.8750 mills for FY 2026-27, down from 4.9750 the year before. Each mill means a dollar of tax for every thousand of taxable value. The council has trimmed the rate for eleven years running, from 6.6289 in FY 2015/16, a drop of about 25 percent.

The city controls just two lines on your bill: its own rate and the voter-approved debt for the Crosstown Parkway, together about 21 percent of a total bill. The other 14 lines belong to the county, school board, water management district and special districts.

Your bill can still climb when the city rate falls. Taxable value may have risen faster, another authority may have raised its rate, or you may have lost an exemption.

Due dates, discounts and installments

Bills go out on or about November 1. Pay in November and you save 4 percent. The gross amount is due through March 31. Payments received from April 1 onward count as late and carry penalties.

Delinquent taxes and the certificate sale

Miss the March 31 cutoff and the bill is delinquent from April 1, with interest and fees starting. What stays unpaid is offered at the Tax Collector's yearly certificate sale, where bidding opens in May.

To stop a certificate, payment has to be in by five in the evening on the last business day before June 1. Certificates issue on June 1 or the business day after. Online payments shut off at that hour and reopen after processing, usually by mid-June. A payment counts when received, not when postmarked.

  • A certificate doesn't cost you the house, but extra interest and fees apply, and it can later support a tax deed application.

A relative, lender or friend can pay a delinquent bill for you. Doing so gives them no ownership stake.

How a sale changes the tax

Once the deed records, the appraiser is free to reset the house to full just value on the following January 1, and your exemptions don't pass to the new owner. Your exemption and Save Our Homes benefit linger on the parcel through the year of purchase, which is why a buyer's first bill can look gentler than the second.

A buyer who lives in the home on January 1 and files for homestead by March 1 gets the exemption that year, though the cap does not start until the following year. The assessment cap is the lower of 3% or CPI, and the figure is 2.7% for 2026.

Deed stamps run $0.70 per $100 of price. The contract may assign the cost to one side, yet each name on the deed can be pursued for it. The Clerk collects at recording. Ask your closing agent to order the tax payoff and say whether this year's bill is already settled.

Homestead and portability

Own the home and live in it as of January 1, then apply to the county appraiser before March 1. The first $25,000 applies to every levy including school taxes. The additional exemption reaches non-school taxes only.

Moving within Florida can carry a benefit. Portability lets a mover take up to $500,000 of the Save Our Homes savings to a new homestead. The window is three years, counted from January 1 of the year the old homestead ended.

Extra reductions exist for seniors and for people with disabilities. Homestead ends once the house is rented or stops being your permanent residence, so tell the appraiser instead of waiting for a review.

Checks before closing

Look up the parcel on the appraiser's site and confirm that the exemption and value shown are right. Next, collect the Tax Collector's balance for the current year plus any earlier ones, and pass both numbers to the closing agent. If your mailing address changed, update it with the appraiser so notices reach you.

If the bill seems large after a recent reassessment, compare it with the appraiser's tax estimator. TRIM notices show each authority's proposed rate before final rates are certified in the fall. A value dispute goes through the Value Adjustment Board forms on the appraiser's site, and the petition window is 25 days after the TRIM notice goes out.

Selling with taxes owed

Owing taxes doesn't block a sale. Your title company or closing agent asks for a payoff figure, and what you owe is deducted from your sale proceeds.

A few simple habits help. Ask for the payoff in writing, and request a fresh one if closing slips. Keep the payoff letter and the final settlement statement together with your sale papers. Tell your agent or buyer about unpaid special assessments or an installment plan still running. A cash buyer skips lender appraisal and underwriting delays, but the tax payoff and deed taxes are settled the same way at the closing table.

Frequently asked questions

Who controls the Port St. Lucie tax rate?

The City Council sets only the city's own rate, 4.8750 mills for FY 2026-27. The county, school board and other authorities set the other lines on your bill.

When do Port St. Lucie taxes go delinquent?

April 1. St. Lucie County bills are due by March 31, and unpaid taxes go into the certificate sale that opens in May.

Does St. Lucie County allow installments?

Yes. The application closes April 30 and the estimated bill must top $100. Expect 6%, 4.5% and 3% discounts on the first three payments.

How do I get the homestead exemption?

File with the St. Lucie County Property Appraiser by March 1, once you own the home and live in it on the January 1 assessment date. The appraiser has an online portal and two offices.

Can a late payment stop a tax certificate?

Only if the Tax Collector has it by five in the evening on the last business day before June 1. A later payment can't stop the certificate, even when mailed earlier.
